intro_body: We want to understand how different people perceive the probability of extraterrestrial life existing in the universe. This is an open test: anyone can take part, with no sign-up, and compare their estimate with other participants.
intro_eq_body: In 1961, Frank Drake composed a Fermi estimate — an equation to estimate N, the number of detectable extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way, and instigate the discussion of the scientific community about the existence of extraterrestrial life. It multiplies seven parameters, each representing a step on the path from star formation to interstellar communication and detection. Different versions of this equation have been proposed over time. Here, we will use the Carl Sagan's version, that starts with the number of stars in the Milky Way.
intro_why_body: The values of the parameters are deeply uncertain and depend on very different areas of knowledge — astrophysics, biology, cognitive sciences. That is why we ask for a probability distribution, not a single number.
intro_step1: For each parameter, you will move a slider that defines a probability distribution — not a single value, but the range of values you consider plausible and how likely each one is. Be careful that the horizontal axis is logarithmic.
intro_step2: At the end, your personal distribution of N is calculated right here in your browser and compared with the participants'.
intro_step3: Your answers will be published as open data. The participants' curve is updated once a month; bookmark the results page to see your distribution again.
intro_demo_caption: Drag the centre handle (■) to move the peak and the side handles (○) to adjust uncertainty.
consent_what_body: This is an open test, maintained by Fernando Mello, in which anyone can estimate the parameters of the Drake Equation. Submitted answers are published as open data and used to show the distribution of participants.
consent_data_1: Your probability distributions for each parameter of the Drake Equation
consent_data_2: Optional answers: country, field of study (broad and specific), familiarity with astronomy and biology, whether you took the test before, and beliefs about life in the universe
consent_data_3: Language, date of submission (no time of day) and a random identifier generated in your browser
consent_data_4: We do not ask for your name or e-mail and we do not publish IP addresses. The form service that receives the answers (Google) may log technical data such as the IP address, under its own policies.
consent_rights_title: Your rights and what this means
consent_rights_1: Voluntary participation — you may stop at any time before submitting
consent_rights_2: Public and irrevocable — once submitted, your answers sit in a public repository under the CC BY 4.0 license: anyone may copy and reuse them, with attribution. They cannot be removed or changed afterwards, including in copies we do not control
consent_rights_3: Anonymous is not absolute — we publish no name, e-mail or time of day, but the combination of country, field and answers could, in principle, identify you to someone who already knows those answers. All context fields are optional: answer only what you are comfortable making public
consent_rights_4: Open use — the data may be used for academic, educational or recreational purposes
consent_chk1: I have read and understood the information above.
consent_chk2: I am 18 or older and I take part voluntarily.
consent_chk3: I understand that my answers will be published as open data (CC BY 4.0) and cannot be removed later.
